verdict.justification: Both deliberate deviations are CORRECT and I verified the reasoning by probe: CR5's `fromId` rule is the only one that keeps the legitimate asker's wait and refuses every foreign question (a `toId` rule would do the opposite on both counts), and CR3's split — session id on `fromId`, durable address on `fromMemberId` plus `selfId`/`issuerId`/ack/unread — closes all four named consequences for a lineage-only captain while a non-captain stays refused and an ordinary member is unchanged. T26's freeze is real: the live assertion is green with zero unfrozen/stale, and all ELEVEN entries match their actual specifiers. Eight gates green including dist-fresh. One Nit (a reseed edge in the CR5 match).

judgements.item: CR5 — the writer implemented the target-ownership rule on `fromId` instead of CodeRabbit's suggested `toId`
judgements.evidence: Probe: the holder's own question passes whether the row's `fromId` is the session id or the roster id; ANOTHER member's question is refused `foreign-target` naming the sender; the CR-described case — a question ADDRESSED to the holder but SENT by someone else — is refused `foreign-target` too (a `toId` rule would ADMIT it). And the legitimate question's `toId` is the ANSWERER, not the holder (`toIdRuleWouldRefuseLegitimate:true`), so CodeRabbit's rule would refuse the shipped member→captain wait. The refusal is `foreign-target`, carries no label list, and no row is written.

judgements.item: CR3 — the writer kept `fromId` = the caller's SESSION id and applied the durable address to `fromMemberId` (and to `selfId`/`issuerId`/ack/unread) instead of CodeRabbit's `fromId: callerAddress`
judgements.evidence: Probes with the exact values the tool now passes: (a) ack of a lead-addressed row by `byId = leadId` → moved; (b) `*` from the lineage captain with `selfId = leadId` → targets [M1, M2], the lead's own row excluded; (c) the captain's own question (fromId = resumed session, fromMemberId = leadId) answered to the durable `leadId` → ok (the store's sender/asker sets union both spellings); (d) a permit issued with `issuerId = leadId` validates without `foreign-issuer`. Non-captain: a stranger's ack is refused, a foreign answer is `not-recipient`, a permit from a non-lead is `foreign-issuer`. Ordinary member: its ack still moves. The protocol's `MailMessage.fromId` is documented as a session id, so keeping the session there loses nothing.

t26Audit.evidence: The live assertion `expect({unfrozen: result.unfrozen.map(identityOf), stale: result.stale}).toEqual({unfrozen: [], stale: []})` runs green; the file's fixture arms prove an extra coupling reddens and a stale entry reddens. I independently spot-checked ALL ELEVEN frozen entries against their real source specifiers: 11/11 matched (`matched=11 missing=0`).

findings.title: The CR5 target-ownership match reads only `target.fromId`, not the row's `fromMemberId`, so a holder RESEEDED within the permit's TTL cannot wait on its own pre-reseed question
findings.what: Probe: a question sent by the holder under its OLD session (row `fromMemberId: "M1"`) is refused `foreign-target` after the holder's session is re-minted — and the refusal names the holder itself ('was sent by "Senior Engineer"'). Everywhere else the ownership rules match BOTH recorded spellings (the store's `senderIds` unions `fromId` and `fromMemberId`), so this one path is stricter than the rest.
findings.why: It is an edge (the reseed must land between asking and a TTL-bounded wait), but it is the same D16c two-spellings class the repository fixed elsewhere, and the sentence is confusing because the sender and the holder share a name.
findings.direction: Match the row's `fromMemberId` too — `spellings.has(target.fromId) || (target.fromMemberId !== undefined && spellings.has(target.fromMemberId))` — a one-line change with the same semantics the store already uses. Optional for this wave; the main cases are correct.
